acheng.1.tier_reason: Core: almost every Ah Cheng-style piece starts this way, and the rest of the restraint depends on it.
acheng.1.why: The reader opens their eyes already standing on the scene, without sitting through a lecture first. With no background given, they have to find it in the actions, and that grabs their attention. The summary you skip at the start leaks out bit by bit later, which is more convincing than stating it.
acheng.1.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *The Chess King* opens straight on the chaos of a station send-off: voices, crowding, luggage, and not one sentence about the era.
>
> *Demonstration:* The night shift at the factory lets out at twelve. Out the gate, two hundred paces east, there is a noodle stall under the bridge.
acheng.1.breakdown:
- “The night shift lets out at twelve”: a point in time that also tells you what the people do.
- “Two hundred paces east”: direction and distance, as if someone is walking and the camera follows.
- “A noodle stall”: the first paragraph already lands on the thing the whole piece is about.
- Not one adjective, no “in those days”.
acheng.1.overdo:
> It was an era of material scarcity yet full of warmth, and the city nights always felt especially long. Deep in my memory there is a little noodle stall…

The fault: it sets the tone of the era first, then turns lyrical with “deep in my memory”. The feeling arrives before the scene does.
acheng.1.when_not:
- When readers know nothing of the background and cannot follow without it (a historical narrative for foreign readers, say), give one line of context.
- Expository writing and news leads, which need the main point first.
acheng.1.exercise: Write the first two sentences of a short piece. They must contain a place and a specific time or distance. The words “era”, “memory” and “back then” are not allowed.
acheng.1.check: You can point to a specific object or place in the first sentence.
acheng.1.adjacent:
- wangxiaobo.2: opening on a small personal event carries a chatty tone and leads into argument.
- acheng.10: the cold close is the same restraint applied to the ending.

acheng.2.tier_reason: Signature: the eating scene is the passage readers most associate with Ah Cheng.
acheng.2.why: “Delicious” is the author telling the reader; actions are something the reader sees. If a man pauses after a sip of soup and picks every grain of rice clean, nobody needs to say he has known hunger or how much this bowl weighs. The slower and finer the actions, the heavier they become.
acheng.2.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *The Chess King* follows a man eating, from picking up the bowl to gathering the grains that fell, in a minutely detailed chain of actions. It is one of the best-known passages in the story.
>
> *Demonstration:* Soup first. One sip, a pause, let it go down the throat. Then the noodles, one chopsticks-load at a time, rested on the rim so the soup drips back into the bowl, then into the mouth.
acheng.2.breakdown:
- “First… then…”: there is an order, like a ritual.
- “A pause”: a stop inside the action, and the stop is the cherishing.
- “Rested on the rim so the soup drips back”: not a drop wasted, so hunger needs no mention.
- The whole passage has no “fragrant”, no “tasty”.
acheng.2.overdo:
> He wolfed it down with great relish, as if it were the most delicious bowl of noodles in the world, every mouthful full of the taste of happiness.

The fault: two set phrases and a simile, zero actions. The reader sees nothing.
acheng.2.when_not:
- When eating is not what matters in the piece; a string of fine actions will upstage the main thing.
- Leisurely connoisseurship or writing about ingredients and how to cook them (that is wangzengqi-writing's job).
acheng.2.exercise: Write yourself eating something, with at least four consecutive actions and no flavour adjectives at all.
acheng.2.check: Remove the character's name and the reader can still tell from the actions whether this person is hungry.
acheng.2.adjacent:
- acheng.3: action for thought is the general principle; the eating scene is its extreme case.
- acheng.9: the Way in the common often uses eating as its “common” end.

acheng.3.tier_reason: Core: it runs through the whole piece and holds up most of the other atoms.
acheng.3.why: “He was moved” is a conclusion the reader can only accept; “he was wiping the wok” is evidence the reader has to work from. Feeling the reader works out is deeper and more believable than feeling they are told. When the narrator stays out of the characters' heads, the characters seem to have measure and dignity.
acheng.3.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *The Chess King* and *King of the Children* hardly ever enter a character's mind; the feeling sits in the gaps between actions and dialogue.
>
> *Demonstration:* The bowl was pushed over, a fried egg hidden at the bottom. I looked at him. He was wiping the wok.
acheng.3.breakdown:
- “Hidden at the bottom”: the kindness is given covertly, never stated.
- “I looked at him”: all of the narrator's question and gratitude sits in one look.
- “He was wiping the wok”: the reply is no reply; he sidesteps the thanks.
- Three sentences, not one verb of thought or feeling.
acheng.3.overdo:
> Seeing the egg at the bottom of the bowl, a wave of warmth rose in my heart and my eyes grew moist. I knew he was quietly caring for me in his own way.

The fault: it translates action into thought and explains the motive as well, leaving the reader no gap to fill.
acheng.3.when_not:
- When the thinking is itself the plot (detection, inner struggle).
- When the action is too vague for the reader to infer the feeling; find a more precise action, or add a line.
acheng.3.exercise: Rewrite “she was nervous” as two actions, with no emotion words.
acheng.3.check: The passage has no “thought”, “felt”, “sensed” or “in her heart”, yet the reader can still name the character's feeling.
acheng.3.adjacent:
- acheng.2: the eating scene is its specialised form.
- acheng.8: heavy things lightly also speaks through traces, but for the heaviest event, not everyday feeling.

acheng.4.tier_reason: Common: used whenever a minor character needs to stand up fast.
acheng.4.why: Readers remember a person by one nail: two missing fingers, one odd remark. One nail sticks better than a pile of adjectives. Because the author doesn't explain, readers get curious, and give the person a little more respect and a little more guessing.
acheng.4.example:
> *Paraphrase:* In *King of the Children* a pupil is established by one stubborn act; most of the supporting cast in *The Chess King* gets a stroke or two.
>
> *Demonstration:* His name was Sun, and his left hand was two fingers short. Someone once asked. He said, “Sharpening knives.” The person asked no more.
acheng.4.breakdown:
- “His name was Sun”: a surname, no history.
- “Two fingers short”: a physical nail you can't forget.
- “Sharpening knives”: two words that hold the craft, the hardship and the toughness.
- “The person asked no more”: someone else's reaction passes judgment for the narrator.
acheng.4.overdo:
> Master Sun was about fifty, lean, dark-skinned and steady-eyed, a taciturn, hard-working, kind-hearted old craftsman.

The fault: a list of looks plus three character adjectives. The reader remembers none of them.
acheng.4.when_not:
- When a main character must unfold in layers and change; one line can't hold them.
- In an ensemble where everyone gets only one line, it turns into a roll call.
acheng.4.exercise: Write a two-sentence entrance for someone you know: one habit or physical trait, plus one thing they once said.
acheng.4.check: Nothing later in the text explains what kind of person this is.
acheng.4.adjacent:
- acheng.5: plain dialogue often supplies the one line.
- acheng.6: folk wisdom also has a character speak, but to state a truth, not to establish the person.

acheng.5.tier_reason: Common: the default way people talk in this style, used in most scenes with two people.
acheng.5.why: Real speech is short, so cutting it down gives a sense of presence. Without “he said”, readers follow by rhythm, which reads faster and closer. With fewer words, more lives in the gaps: who asks, who doesn't answer, who asks one thing more. The whole relationship is there.
acheng.5.example:
> *Paraphrase:* The exchanges between the narrator and others in *The Chess King* are mostly short lines back and forth, without speech tags.
>
> *Demonstration:*
> “Large?”
> “Large.”
> “Egg?”
acheng.5.breakdown:
- One word each; the asker even drops the subject, practised and cool.
- “Large.”: the answer repeats the question, the most economical reply.
- No answer after “Egg?”: next the narrator feels his pocket and says no; the shortage of money shows in the pause.
- Not one “said”.
acheng.5.overdo:
> “Young man, do you want a large bowl or a small one?” the owner asked warmly. “Large, I guess!” I answered, a bit embarrassed, counting the money in my pocket in my head.

The fault: the dialogue is stretched, the tags carry adverbs, and thoughts are added. Every unspoken measure has been spelled out.
acheng.5.when_not:
- In multi-person dialogue, dropping all tags leaves readers unsure who is speaking.
- When dialogue must carry a lot of information (plot setup, explaining rules).
acheng.5.exercise: Write a dialogue about buying something: six exchanges, each line no more than four words, at least four lines without “said”.
acheng.5.check: Readers can tell who says each line, and can read the relationship between the two.
acheng.5.adjacent:
- acheng.4: one line makes a person often takes its line from the dialogue.
- acheng.3: action for thought often fills the gaps in the dialogue.

acheng.6.tier_reason: Signature: the one homely truth per piece is a distinctly Ah Cheng move.
acheng.6.why: A truth from the author's mouth is preaching; from the old gatekeeper's mouth it is experience. Homely words are short and incomplete, so readers have to chew on them. When the narrator doesn't respond, the line hangs, and the longer it hangs the heavier it gets. It only holds its weight if it appears once in the whole piece.
acheng.6.example:
> *Paraphrase:* In *The Chess King* an unremarkable old man talks about the way of chess; it is where the piece's Way lies, yet the narrator adds no comment.
>
> *Demonstration:* He finished the last blade, glanced at me and said, “A knife doesn't mind going dull. It minds nobody using it.” I didn't understand. I nodded.
acheng.6.breakdown:
- “Finished the last blade”: the truth comes after the work, not as a lesson.
- “A knife doesn't mind going dull…”: the words are plain, the meaning turns toward people but is never spelled out.
- “I didn't understand. I nodded”: the narrator doesn't take it up, and even admits not understanding.
acheng.6.overdo:
> The old man said earnestly, “Life is like sharpening a knife: only through grinding do you become sharp.” Those words have benefited me all my life and still inspire me today.

The fault: the homely line has become a maxim, and the narrator adds “benefited me all my life”. The truth is chewed up and spoon-fed.
acheng.6.when_not:
- When the piece already has one; a second makes it a collection of aphorisms.
- When the speaker doesn't fit the line (a child saying something worldly-wise); it will ring false.
acheng.6.exercise: Write one line a craftsman says after finishing work, no more than ten words, in the language of his trade, followed only by an action.
acheng.6.check: What immediately follows the line is an action, not a judgment.
acheng.6.adjacent:
- acheng.9: the Way in the common is a structural juxtaposition; folk wisdom is a single line.
- wangxiaobo.5: in the measure of interest the narrator states his own standard; Ah Cheng never lets the narrator do that.

acheng.7.tier_reason: Signature: the classical rhythm under vernacular words is the sound of Ah Cheng's prose.
acheng.7.why: Vernacular prose is soft and sags when it runs long. A short, tight sentence at the end of a paragraph props it up like a bone, and the paragraph stands. Readers pause there, and the rhythm gets its rise and fall. It only feels hard if used in a few places; spread over the whole piece it becomes a mannerism.
acheng.7.example:
> *Paraphrase:* The sketch-like short pieces of *Romance of the Land* have the shortest sentences and the hardest endings; the same closing move is common in the novellas too.
>
> *Demonstration:* The price stayed. Some found it dear. He didn't argue.
acheng.7.breakdown:
- “The price stayed”: subject and verb, cut to the bone.
- “Some found it dear”: the matter turns.
- “He didn't argue”: it closes, and the man's temper settles.
- All ordinary words, no archaic particles.
acheng.7.overdo:
> I beheld the man and marvelled thereat. The price unchanged, the customer deeming it dear, nor did he contend, for such was his nature.

The fault: it imitates antiquity with classical particles. All tone, no bone; readers only feel the pose.
acheng.7.when_not:
- Spread over the whole text, it reads like a telegram or a pastiche.
- In dialogue, it makes characters sound unlike people.
acheng.7.exercise: Take a narrative paragraph you have written and change only its last sentence into two or three short sentences of four words or fewer, all in plain words.
acheng.7.check: No more than five such closings in the whole text, and not one archaic particle.
acheng.7.adjacent: - acheng.10: the cold close is also short, but it governs the content of the ending (stopping on an action); classical bones governs sentence rhythm.

acheng.8.tier_reason: Common: used at the one heaviest moment of a story, not in every paragraph.
acheng.8.why: If the author pours effort into the heavy part, readers either weep on cue or recoil. If the author gives only a trace, readers have to fill the blank themselves, with their own experience, so it hurts more. Writing it lightly is also a way of respecting suffering, not putting it on show.
acheng.8.example:
> *Paraphrase:* In *The Chess King* and *The King of Trees* the heaviest turns are written very briefly, and the text soon returns to what is in front of it.
>
> *Demonstration:* That winter the factory shut. I went to the bridge once. The tricycle wasn't there. There was a black patch on the ground, burned by the stove.
acheng.8.breakdown:
- “The factory shut”: one line for the biggest event, no consequences.
- “I went once”: action in place of missing someone.
- “A black patch on the ground”: only a trace; where the man went is never said.
- No “never again”, no “forever”.
acheng.8.overdo:
> That winter the factory went bankrupt and countless workers lost their livelihoods. I never saw Old Geng again; that warm noodle stall vanished forever into the cold wind, vanished into my youth.

The fault: “countless”, “never again” and “forever” pile up, with lyricism on top. Every blank has been filled in.
acheng.8.when_not:
- When readers need the factual details (nonfiction, reporting); lightness becomes vagueness.
- When the groundwork is too thin for readers to know how heavy the event is; a light touch gets missed.
acheng.8.exercise: Write a loss: one sentence to state what happened, one sentence for something left behind afterwards.
acheng.8.check: The heaviest event takes fewer words than the everyday matter in the paragraph before it.
acheng.8.adjacent:
- acheng.3: action for thought handles everyday feeling; heavy things lightly handles the single heaviest blow.
- wangxiaobo.9: saying the absurd calmly also lowers the voice, but for comedy.

acheng.9.tier_reason: Signature: setting eating beside chess, the common beside the Way, is the structure Ah Cheng is known for.
acheng.9.why: Write only the common and the piece stays grounded but low; write only the Way and it is lofty but empty. Side by side, readers see the Way growing out of eating one's fill and earning a living, and the common things gain weight too. The author doesn't rank them; readers weigh them.
acheng.9.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *The Chess King* sets eating beside chess; in *King of the Children* a dictionary carries enormous weight; *The King of Trees* writes people and trees.
>
> *Demonstration:* A knife was five yuan. … Master Sun spent half an hour on it, then wouldn't take payment. “It's a good knife. Sharpening it, I'm the one getting the bargain.”
acheng.9.breakdown:
- “Five yuan”: the common end, the price stated plainly.
- “Half an hour”: the Way end, the time a craftsman is willing to spend.
- “Wouldn't take payment”, “I'm the one getting the bargain”: the sum is reversed, craft outweighs money, but no one says so.
acheng.9.overdo:
> Though materially poor, they were spiritually rich. Beyond daily necessities, craft carried their longing for a better life.

The fault: it becomes a “materially poor, spiritually rich” contrast essay, turning side-by-side into a ranking.
acheng.9.when_not:
- When a short piece can't carry two lines; forcing them together looks pasted.
- When the Way side has no concrete action and is left as a concept.
acheng.9.exercise: Write three sentences: the price of something, the effort a person spends on it, and one unexpected decision they make.
acheng.9.check: Nowhere in the text is there a sentence comparing which is higher, the common or the Way.
acheng.9.adjacent:
- acheng.6: folk wisdom points to the Way in one line; the Way in the common is the structure of the whole piece.
- acheng.2: the eating scene often serves as the common end.

acheng.10.tier_reason: Core: the ending sets the flavour of the whole piece, and every Ah Cheng-style story needs one.
acheng.10.why: Readers have been walked through the whole story; if the author sighs at the end, their feeling is fixed into shape. If the author just turns and walks off, the feeling stays in the reader's hands and grows heavier with thought. The ending decides the taste of the piece; one sigh can undo all the words saved before it.
acheng.10.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *The Chess King* and *King of the Children* both end on very ordinary scenes, with no summing up.
>
> *Demonstration:* I stood there a while, then walked back.
acheng.10.breakdown:
- “Stood there a while”: the feeling takes up only a pause.
- “Walked back”: the most ordinary action, and the person leaves.
- Two actions, zero judgments, no exclamation mark.
acheng.10.overdo:
> I will never forget the taste of that bowl of noodles. So the simplest warmth in life was hidden in a bowl of hot noodle soup all along.

The fault: “I will never forget” and a “so it was…” uplift finish the reader's feeling for them.
acheng.10.when_not:
- Genres that need a clear conclusion (reports, commentary).
- When the body isn't fully written; a cold close then just looks unfinished.
acheng.10.exercise: Give a narrative you have written a new ending: at most three sentences, only one action or one ordinary line.
acheng.10.check: The last paragraph has three sentences or fewer, no evaluative words, no exclamation marks.
acheng.10.adjacent:
- wangxiaobo.10: the playful close smiles and closes along the line of reasoning; the cold close doesn't smile and stops on an action.
- acheng.8: heavy things lightly often sits right before the cold close.
